## Foundations: SIR theory and the Julia workflow — Day 1, Session 2

Worksheet: `worksheets/02-foundations-sir-theory-and-the-julia-workflow.qmd`. The chapter is
[Foundations](../chapters/01-foundations.qmd).

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-setup
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using NonlinearSolve
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end

u0    = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]                          # S(0), I(0), R(0)
p     = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
tspan = (0.0, 80.0)

println("kernel ready; R₀ = ", p.β * p.c / p.γ)
```

### Part A — solve it, then read the answer

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-a1
prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p)
sol  = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)

check("the solver ran", sol.retcode == ReturnCode.Success)
check("it stored one state every half day", length(sol.t) == 161)

sol.u[end]
```

The kernel goes in by name: `sir_ode!`, not `sir_ode!(...)`. The solver calls it
thousands of times with its own arguments, so what it needs is the function
itself.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-a2
t = sol.t
S = sol[1, :]
I = sol[2, :]
R = sol[3, :]

check("one value of I per stored time", length(I) == length(t))
check("the epidemic took off", maximum(I) > u0[2])
check("nobody is created or destroyed",
      all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), p.N; atol = 1e-6), sol.u))

println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(I), digits = 1),
        " on day ", round(t[argmax(I)], digits = 1))
println("largest conservation error: ", maximum(abs(sum(u) - p.N) for u in sol.u))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch01-sir
#| fig-cap: "Baseline SIR epidemic: susceptible, infectious and recovered over 80 days."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "number of individuals")
lines!(ax, t, S; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "S")
lines!(ax, t, I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "I")
lines!(ax, t, R; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3, label = "R")
axislegend(ax; position = :rc)
fig
```

#### A1. Interpret

- `lines!` needs a plain list of numbers, one per time, which is what
  `sol[2, :]` gives. `sol.u` is a vector of 161 *state vectors*, so its first
  element is `[990.0, 10.0, 0.0]`, not a number. Both hold the same data:
  `sol.u` slices it by time, `sol[i, :]` by compartment.
- The conservation error is arithmetic, not modelling. `Tsit5` combines several
  derivative evaluations per step with floating-point weights, and the rounding
  does not cancel, so $S + I + R$ drifts from $N$ by order $10^{-13}$ people over
  80 days — a few parts in $10^{16}$ of $N$, the floor set by double precision.
- The cell prints the largest drift rather than quoting a figure, because the
  exact value moves with the solver, its tolerances and the package versions.
- The check's $10^{-6}$ tolerance is six orders of magnitude looser than that
  floor: it is there to catch a mistyped equation, not to measure the solver.
  Tightening `reltol`/`abstol` shrinks the discretisation error but not the
  rounding floor.
- Conservation holds because it is a property of the equations, not something the
  code enforces. The three right-hand sides sum to zero by construction, since
  every flow leaves one compartment and enters another, and a quantity with zero
  derivative does not change. A typo in `du[2]` almost always breaks it.

### Part B — the threshold, and when nothing happens

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-b1
R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ

peak_index = argmax(I)
S_over_N_at_peak = S[peak_index] / p.N

check("R₀ is 2 for the baseline", isapprox(R₀, 2.0; atol = 1e-9))
check("the peak sits on the threshold",
      isapprox(S_over_N_at_peak, 1 / R₀; rtol = 0.01))   # 1% relative

(R₀ = R₀, threshold = 1 / R₀, S_over_N_at_peak = S_over_N_at_peak)
```

- The susceptible fraction at the peak lands on $0.5 = 1/R_0$ within tolerance.
  It is inexact only because the solution was stored every half day, so `argmax`
  finds the largest *stored* value; the ordinary differential equations session
  locates the peak exactly with a callback.
- The equality describes a run that grows before it turns over, here
  $R_0 S(0)/N = 1.98$. The $c = 4$ run below has no such crossing: $I$ falls from
  day zero, its largest stored value is $I(0)$, and $S/N$ there is $0.99$.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-b2
contact_rates = [4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0]
results = map(contact_rates) do c_val
    p_c = merge(p, (c = c_val,))
    s   = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p_c), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5)
    (c = c_val,
     R₀ = round(p_c.β * p_c.c / p_c.γ; digits = 2),
     peak_I = round(maximum(s[2, :]); digits = 1),
     infected_by_80 = round(1 - s[1, end] / p_c.N; digits = 3))   # no longer susceptible
end

check("each run used its own contact rate",
      length(unique(r.R₀ for r in results)) == 4)
check("c = 4 gives R₀ below 1", results[1].R₀ < 1)
check("prevalence does not grow at c = 4", results[1].peak_I <= u0[2])
check("the day-80 total climbs with contact rate",
      let a = [r.infected_by_80 for r in results]; issorted(a) && allunique(a) end)

results
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch01-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Infectious curves across contact rates. Below c ≈ 5.05 the initial infections fade without an epidemic: with 99% susceptible at the start, growth needs R₀S(0)/N > 1, which is a little more than R₀ > 1."
fig2 = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax2  = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
            title = "Contact rate and the epidemic threshold")
for c_val in contact_rates
    s = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, merge(p, (c = c_val,))), Tsit5();
              saveat = 0.5)
    lines!(ax2, s.t, s[2, :]; linewidth = 3, label = "c = $(Int(c_val))")
end
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt)
fig2
```

#### B1. Interpret

- At $c = 4$ the ten initial infectious people do infect others before they
  recover, so the attack rate is not zero. What is missing is *growth*: each
  infection produces fewer than one further infection, so each generation is
  smaller and the chain dies out. "No epidemic" means no self-sustaining
  transmission, not no transmission — and early case counts look similar either
  way, so what separates them is the trend, not the level.
- $R_0 = 1$ at $c = 5$, but that is the threshold for a *fully* susceptible
  population. With 1% already infectious, prevalence grows only when
  $R_0 S(0)/N > 1$, needing $c > \gamma/(\beta s_0) \approx 5.05$ where
  $s_0 = 0.99$. At $c = 5$ the product is $0.99$ and $I$ declines from day zero.
- The threshold depends on how many remain susceptible, not on how many are
  currently infectious. So a falling case count and a controlled epidemic are
  different claims: a fall caused by using up susceptibles holds as long as $S/N$
  stays below the $1/R_0$ that returns when control ends, while a fall bought by
  control can reverse, because the susceptibles it protected are still there.
  Case counts alone do not separate the two.
- The steepest gains are near $R_0 = 1$. Between $c = 4$ and $c = 6$ the day-80
  total moves from 4.5% to 32.7%; the same step from $c = 8$ to $c = 10$ moves it
  from 65% to 80%, and adding $c = 20$ reaches 98%, so doubling transmission from
  the baseline buys only 18 more points.
- Final size is not the whole story. Over that same $c = 8$ to $c = 10$ range the
  *peak* goes from 88 to 158, and the peak is what determines whether hospitals
  cope. Cutting $c$ from 10 to 8 leaves $R_0$ at 1.6, well above 1, yet spares
  about 15% of the population an infection while nearly halving the peak. An
  intervention too weak to reach the threshold still changes the picture, and a
  decision usually rests on both numbers.

::: {.callout-note}
The column is `infected_by_80`, computed as $1 - S(80)/N$, rather than
`attack_rate`, and the distinction is not cosmetic.

- It counts everyone no longer susceptible at day 80, whether recovered or still
  infectious. $R(80)/N$ would miss the ones still infectious, which matters
  exactly when the epidemic has not finished.
- At $c = 6$ the three numbers separate: $R(80)/N = 0.321$, infected by day 80 is
  $0.327$, and the eventual attack rate is $0.348$. At $c = 10$ the epidemic is
  over by day 80 and all three agree to three figures.
- Part C computes the final size directly, without simulating.
:::

### Part C — the final size, without simulating

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-c1
s₀ = u0[1] / p.N

residual(s, R0) = s - s₀ * exp(-R0 * (1 - s))
fs_prob = NonlinearProblem(residual, 0.2, R₀)

s_inf = solve(fs_prob, NewtonRaphson()).u
attack_rate = 1 - s_inf

check("s∞ is a fraction, smaller than s₀", 0 < s_inf < s₀)
check("it really is a root", isapprox(residual(s_inf, R₀), 0.0; atol = 1e-8))

sol_long = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (0.0, 400.0), p), Tsit5();
                 reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10, save_everystep = false)
simulated = sol_long.u[end][1] / p.N

check("analytic and simulated agree", isapprox(s_inf, simulated; atol = 1e-3))

(s_infinity = round(s_inf; digits = 4),
 simulated = round(simulated; digits = 4),
 attack_rate = round(attack_rate; digits = 4))
```

The starting guess is not a free choice: the equation has a second root above 1,
and a large guess such as $0.9$ converges to that one.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch01-c2
turning_point = 1 - log(s₀ * R₀) / R₀

for guess in (0.2, 0.65, turning_point, 0.9)
    s = solve(NonlinearProblem(residual, guess, R₀), NewtonRaphson())
    println("guess ", rpad(round(guess; digits = 4), 8),
            " value ", rpad(round(s.u; digits = 6), 10),
            " residual ", rpad(round(residual(s.u, R₀); digits = 6), 10),
            " ", s.retcode)
end
```

- The residual turns over at $s = 1 - \ln(s_0 R_0)/R_0 \approx 0.658$, which is
  what puts two roots there. That explains why there are two roots, not which
  guess ends at which one.
- Starting exactly on the turning point shows the difference: the slope is zero,
  Newton's first step is undefined, and the solve fails instead of reaching
  either root — the value returned is the guess itself, with a residual of $0.16$.
- The value and the residual are what identify a root. The return code is a
  useful signal alongside them, though which code a failure produces can change
  between package versions, which makes it a weak thing to build a check
  around.
- Both converged values solve the equation, but only one can be a susceptible
  fraction: $s_\infty = 1.010$ would mean more people finished susceptible than
  started. That is why the worksheet checks $0 < s_\infty < s_0$, a stronger test
  than `retcode = Success`, which the root above 1 earns too. Deciding which root
  is the epidemic is the modeller's job, not the solver's.

#### C1. Interpret

- The epidemic ran out of *infectious people*, not susceptible ones. Once enough
  of the population sits in $R$, the susceptible fraction drops below $1/R_0$ and
  every infection produces less than one replacement, so prevalence falls even
  though 20% could still in principle be infected.
- It overshoots first — transmission does not stop the instant $S/N$ crosses
  $1/R_0$, because a large infectious pool is still working through — and then
  stops well before everyone is reached. The remaining susceptibles are protected
  by the immunity around them, not by anything about themselves.
- The final-size relation collapses $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ into
  $R_0 = \beta c/\gamma$, so any parameter set with the same $R_0$ gives the same
  total. What it discards is *time*.
- Doubling $\beta c$ and $\gamma$ together leaves $R_0$ and the initial state
  alone, so the epidemic traces the same path through $(S, I, R)$ and reaches the
  same peak of 158, but on day 8.8 instead of day 17.5. The wave is narrower, not
  taller: rescaling the rates rescales the clock.
- A wave half as long is a different problem for a health service than one twice
  as long with the same crest, and the final-size relation is silent about both.
  It answers "how many, in the end", not "how fast, and how bad at once", which
  is usually the operational question.
